consumer-nestle-marc-jacobs.headline: Nestlé bets on AI and robotics; Marc Jacobs posts $509m in its last year under LVMH
consumer-nestle-marc-jacobs.body_md:
Two consumer-sector stories sit side by side today, and neither comes with the numbers that would settle it. Nestlé, the world's largest packaged-food group, is reported to be leaning on artificial intelligence and robotics to revive growth. LVMH, meanwhile, is parting with Marc Jacobs, which posted sales of $509m in its final year in the group's portfolio. One is a bet on the factory floor; the other is a pruning of the luxury shelf.

## Nestlé's automation wager

The strategy, as reported by Food Dive, is that automation and AI can help Nestlé restart growth. That is the whole of what can be said with confidence. The triage material carries no spending figures, no growth rates and no named programmes, and Nestlé has not, in the material available, quantified any efficiency gain or revenue effect from the technology.

That gap matters. Large food makers have spent several years trying to restore volume growth after a period in which price rises did much of the work. Automation is one of the few levers wholly within a manufacturer's control: it can lower unit costs, shorten production runs and sharpen demand forecasting. But a lever is only evidence of intent. Until Nestlé puts a figure on savings, throughput or sales uplift, the announcement is a statement of direction, not a result.

The test for peers is simple. If Nestlé can show measurable gains, competitors facing the same volume pressure will have a template to copy. If it cannot, the programme joins a long list of corporate AI narratives that are easy to announce and hard to audit.

## Marc Jacobs, priced on its last LVMH year

WWD reports that Marc Jacobs recorded sales of $509m in its last year in LVMH's portfolio. The brand is being sold, and the figure serves as the base for that sale. What the material does not say is considerable: the buyer, the price and the timing are all absent, and it is unconfirmed whether the $509m is retail or wholesale sales, or which fiscal year it covers. Each of those changes how the number should be read, since a retail figure and a wholesale figure for the same brand can differ widely.

What the sale does suggest is a group choosing focus over breadth. A brand with half a billion dollars in annual sales is not a marginal asset, which makes its exit informative: LVMH appears to be deciding that scale alone does not qualify a label as core. That is an interpretation, not a disclosed rationale, and the group has given none in the material available.

## What ties them together

Both stories are about large consumer groups reshaping where their capital and attention go: Nestlé towards technology inside its plants, LVMH away from a mid-sized fashion name. In each case the missing detail is the one that matters. Nestlé needs a quantified payoff from automation; the Marc Jacobs deal needs a buyer and a price to show what $509m of sales is worth. The next data points are Nestlé's disclosures on productivity and organic growth, and the terms of the Marc Jacobs sale once they are published.
consumer-nestle-marc-jacobs.in_one_sentence: Nestlé is reported to be betting on AI and robotics to revive growth, while LVMH sells Marc Jacobs after a final year of $509m in sales; neither story yet has the figures to judge it.

europe-tiny-cars.headline: Tiny cars take off across Europe as cheap EVs force a price reckoning
europe-tiny-cars.body_md:
Europe's cheapest electric vehicles are no longer a curiosity at the edge of the market. Two kinds of small car now meet there: the quadricycle, which is legally not a car, and the sub-€20,000 city car, which is meant to be one. Both are testing whether volume manufacturers can make money at prices that Chinese entrants are already willing to meet.

## Two routes to a cheap EV

The first route is regulatory. Citroën's Ami, on sale in Europe since 2020, is a two-seat electric quadricycle. That legal category sits below full cars, with lighter safety and performance requirements. It is why the Ami can be priced far below any conventional EV: it carries less car, and less compliance cost.

The second route is to build a proper small car at home for less. Renault's Twingo E-Tech Electric is aimed at a price below €20,000 and is built in Slovenia. Electra, a charging operator, lists a launch price from €19,500 in Evolution trim. The car has a 27.5 kWh LFP battery and a quoted range of up to 263 km, according to Slovenian press. The Slovenian importer expects to sell only 50 to 80 a month in that country. Renault began sales in Slovenia in April 2026, according to an Italian trade-agency report. Reported national incentives, such as a Slovenian grant that Electra says could cut the price to about €15,300 for eligible households, widen the gap further.

The Twingo matters beyond its own volumes. It tests whether a European carmaker can build a small EV in Europe at a price that leaves a margin. Small cars have long been low-margin products, and the cost of batteries and compliance does not scale down with the size of the car.

## The Chinese factor

Chinese brands are expanding in the same space. BYD and Leapmotor are widening their small-EV ranges in Europe, and they compete on price directly with incumbents. One comparison puts the Twingo against BYD's Seagull, sold in some markets as the Dolphin Surf. Motor1 cites about €25,000 as the benchmark for the Renault 5, Fiat Grande Panda and Hyundai Inster, which puts the Twingo's sub-€20,000 target well below the current small-car cluster.

That is the squeeze. Chinese makers arrive with lower cost bases, and a small car is the segment where a price gap is easiest for buyers to see. European incumbents must either match them with cheaper platforms or cede the entry end of the market, where first-time EV buyers are won.

## What to watch

The measure is margin, not volume. Investors in European auto stocks should look for how much Renault, Stellantis, which owns Citroën, and Volkswagen say about unit profitability on their cheapest EVs, and for registration data showing whether Chinese small cars gain share. The next test is Twingo registrations across larger markets than Slovenia. The follow-up is any Chinese response on pricing, including tariff-driven adjustments. If the cheap segment grows but earns little, it would add volume while thinning the margin of the carmakers that build it.

broker-notes-partners-biotech.headline: Barclays turns cautious on Partners Group; investors weigh Democratic drug-pricing risk for biotech
broker-notes-partners-biotech.body_md:
Barclays has turned cautious on Partners Group, the Swiss private-markets manager, and has separately published a view that UK grocery market-share gains will concentrate among a small number of players. Both items come from a single Investing.com summary of broker research. That summary gives no ratings, price targets, figures or company names. The Barclays note itself has not been checked, and a search turned up no independent reporting of it. What follows is therefore a description of what was reported, not a verified account.

## Partners Group: the claim and the missing numbers

According to the summary, the Partners Group downgrade rests on asset sales and redemptions. Those are the two pressure points investors usually watch in private-markets vehicles. Asset sales show whether a manager can return cash to investors at or near stated valuations. Redemptions show how much money investors are asking to take out.

The summary does not say how large either figure is, which funds are involved, or whether Barclays thinks the pressure is rising or just persisting. It also does not say what rating Barclays moved from or to. Without those details the downgrade amounts to one broker's opinion on one stock. If the note quantifies redemption requests or shows that disposals are being made at discounts, it would become a story about liquidity in listed private-markets vehicles. As reported, it is not that story.

## UK grocery: a view without names

The second item is Barclays' expectation that UK grocery share gains will concentrate among a few players. The summary names no companies and gives no data. It is not obviously related to Partners Group.

The view is at least consistent with earlier broker commentary. A Barclays note from late 2025 described a split among UK grocers, with discounters and some premium chains gaining share while mainstream chains struggled. Reporting on that earlier note said Asda was losing shoppers to every major rival and that Lidl was outperforming Aldi. That is background only. Which grocers Barclays has in mind this time is not known.

## Biotech and drug-pricing risk

A separate Investor's Business Daily piece asks whether "anti-pharma" Democrats could cut into a strong run in biotech shares. The candidate material gives no index, period or percentage for the rally. It names no bill, sponsor or date for the drug-pricing push.

The theme is not new. A 2024 IBD analysis argued that expanding the Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare negotiation powers was the biggest policy threat to pharma stocks. Biotech investors lobbied in 2021 and 2022 to extend the negotiation window for small-molecule drugs to 13 years from nine. One investor survey found 76% of respondents expected pricing restrictions to reduce investment in biotech start-ups. Past political remarks have moved the sector quickly: biotech stocks fell about 4.7% after a 2016 Clinton tweet on drug prices.

None of that says what is on the table now. The current proposal and the size of the rally need to be established before the risk can be measured.

## What would settle it

The three threads share one weakness: each is a headline without its figures. For Partners Group, the test is the Barclays note's numbers on redemptions and disposals, along with the company's own reporting. For grocery, it is the names and the share data. For biotech, it is an actual legislative text and a dated price move. Until then the Partners Group downgrade and the grocery call are broker opinions, and the biotech risk is a stated worry that has not been quantified.

huawei-split-verdict.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets, acquitted of racketeering
huawei-split-verdict.body_md:
A federal jury in Brooklyn has delivered a split verdict in the long-running US prosecution of Huawei. According to the BBC, it convicted the Chinese telecoms group of stealing trade secrets but acquitted it of racketeering. The outcome gives the Justice Department a conviction against one of China's best-known technology companies. It also withholds the broadest label prosecutors had sought, that of an organisation run as a criminal enterprise.

This article relies on the BBC's account of the verdict. Counts, the exact charges on which the jury ruled, and any sentencing date had not been independently confirmed from the court record at the time of writing.

## A case nearly a decade in the making

The prosecution grew out of an indictment unsealed in 2020 in the Eastern District of New York. It accused Huawei and affiliates of racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud conspiracy and obstruction. The bank-fraud and obstruction allegations were tied to claims that the company misled financial institutions about its dealings in Iran through a affiliate, Skycom, in breach of US sanctions. The trial opened in September 2026. Reporting indicates that the jury began deliberating on 18 November, with 12 counts in play against Huawei and three affiliated companies.

The trade-secret strand centres on robotics-testing technology taken from T-Mobile US. That background comes from earlier civil and criminal matters, not from this verdict. Separately, a Texas jury found in 2019 that Huawei had misappropriated secrets from the startup CNEX, but it awarded no damages. That was a civil case, but it shows that courts in the US have already heard similar allegations about Huawei's conduct.

## What the split tells us

Racketeering law, known as RICO, was written to reach organised crime. Applied to a corporation, it asserts that the company itself functioned as a vehicle for a pattern of crime, not that individual employees broke rules. That is a high bar. It requires jurors to accept a single connecting story across years of conduct and several continents.

A trade-secret conviction asks for less. Jurors can look at specific acts, such as who obtained particular information, how, and for what use, and decide whether those acts crossed the line. The verdict, as reported, suggests the jury was willing to find that on the narrower question and unwilling to endorse the larger theory. That is an inference from the pattern of outcomes, not from any juror statement, and the reasoning will not be public unless jurors choose to speak.

The defence had argued, among other things, that some of the material described as secret was publicly available. A jury can accept that argument for some counts and not others. A split result does not need a single explanation.

## What follows

Several things now matter. The first is sentencing. A corporation cannot be jailed, so penalties would come in fines, probation conditions or restrictions, and the court's schedule will show how large a consequence this is. The second is appeal. Huawei has contested the case throughout and can be expected to challenge the conviction, and prosecutors will have to decide whether to challenge the acquittal's practical effect on the wider narrative. Acquittals themselves cannot normally be retried.

The third is the policy backdrop. Washington has used export controls, entity listings and criminal cases in parallel against Chinese technology firms. A conviction on IP theft supports the argument that Huawei's conduct warrants those restrictions, while the racketeering acquittal gives the company a line to use in Beijing and in third-country markets. Watch for the sentencing date and for any filing on post-trial motions, which will show how far each side intends to take the dispute.

burnham-veterans-panel-nda.headline: Burnham promises nuclear veterans 'full truth' and signals wider NDA ban
burnham-veterans-panel-nda.body_md:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised British nuclear test veterans the "full truth" about how they were treated, and the government has confirmed an independent panel to examine the matter. That is the account in BBC UK's report. This article could not check the report's text or an official statement, so the panel's remit, membership and timetable are not known here, and quotations are limited to the phrase "full truth" as it appears in the headline.

## A long-running grievance

Between the early 1950s and the mid-1960s Britain tested nuclear weapons in Australia and the Pacific, including at Monte Bello, Emu Field, Maralinga and Christmas Island. Thousands of servicemen took part. Many have since said they were given little protection and poor monitoring. They also say their later illnesses, and in some cases illnesses among their children and grandchildren, were never properly investigated.

Successive governments have mostly argued that the evidence does not show a link between participation and ill health. Campaigners have disputed that for decades. An attempt to bring a group legal claim failed in the courts on time-limit grounds, which left the argument about the facts unresolved. A formal medal for the veterans was introduced only recently, long after most of them had died.

An independent panel is the usual way for a government to move such a dispute out of the department that has defended its position. Whether it counts as a break with the past depends on details not yet available. The questions that matter are whether it can compel documents from the Ministry of Defence, whether it can hear from veterans and families directly, and whether it is asked to look at compensation or only at what happened.

## The NDA signal

The other thread comes from Guardian Politics. It reports Burnham opening the door to a wider ban on non-disclosure agreements in cases of abuse, and describes the moment as a "watershed" on the subject. According to the summary, ministers are signalling they could go beyond their current plans. The Guardian's body text was not available, so the scope, the timing and any direct quotes are unverified. The current plans themselves are not set out here.

The two announcements are different policies, but they have a common theme. Both concern whether people who say they were harmed can get an official account of it. A veteran who was kept uninformed and a former employee bound by a confidentiality clause are in comparable positions. In each case the institution holding the information controls what can be said.

There is also a practical link. A panel looking at decades-old events will rely on witnesses speaking freely, and any confidentiality arrangements or official-secrets constraints on former personnel could limit that. Whether that issue is raised in either announcement is not known.

## What to watch

The first test is the panel's terms of reference: who chairs it, what access to records it gets, and whether it has a reporting date. The second is whether the government publishes legislation or a consultation on the wider NDA ban, since "opening the door" is a weaker commitment than a bill. Until those appear, the "full truth" pledge is a statement of intent, and the veterans' main question, whether anyone will be held to account for how they were treated, remains open.
burnham-veterans-panel-nda.in_one_sentence: Burnham has pledged the 'full truth' to British nuclear test veterans through an independent panel, and reportedly signalled a wider ban on abuse-related NDAs; details remain unconfirmed.

age-of-consent-consultation.headline: Ministers open consultation on the age of consent
age-of-consent-consultation.body_md:
The government has opened a public consultation on the age of consent, asking for views on a legal threshold that has gone unchanged in Britain for more than two decades. The announcement was reported by the BBC. Only that headline and a one-line summary were available when this article was written. The consultation's exact question, scope, closing date and the department running it could not be confirmed, so this article does not guess at them. What is established is the legal background, and a consultation is not a decision.

## What a consultation is, and is not

A UK government consultation invites the public, campaign groups, lawyers and professional bodies to respond to a set of questions, usually over several weeks or months. Ministers then publish a response, which may lead to legislation, to a narrower change, or to nothing. Opening one signals that the government wants evidence or political cover for looking at an issue. It does not commit ministers to a change, and the summary available gives no sign that any decision has been taken.

The age of consent is among the most settled provisions in the criminal law. A consultation that touches it is therefore likely to draw close attention, whatever direction the questions point. Which direction that is has not been verified.

## The law as it stands

In England and Wales the age of consent is 16, set by the Sexual Offences Act 2003. That Act also contains offences that sit alongside the headline age. Sexual activity with a child under 13 is treated as a separate, more serious category in which consent is legally irrelevant. Separate rules cover adults in positions of trust, such as teachers, which apply to people under 18.

Scotland has its own statute. The Sexual Offences (Scotland) Act 2009 also sets the age of consent at 16. Northern Ireland legislates separately too, through the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008. Its age of consent is also 16, not 17 as an early summary of this story suggested. That detail matters because the threshold is the same across the UK but is written into different laws in different legislatures.

The devolution point shapes any reform. Criminal law in Scotland and Northern Ireland is largely devolved, so a change announced at Westminster would not automatically apply across the whole UK. Whether this consultation covers one jurisdiction or several is one of the questions the available material does not answer.

## What to watch

Three things will decide how significant this turns out to be. The first is the wording of the consultation itself: whether it asks open questions about the existing law or puts forward a specific proposal. The second is the closing date, which sets when a government response could appear. The third is how the devolved administrations in Edinburgh and Belfast respond, since any change affecting them would need their own legislative route or agreement.

Until the consultation document is published in full and read, the accurate summary is limited. The government has asked a question about a long-settled law, and the answer, if there is one, is still some way off.

met-police-culture-report.headline: Report finds racism, misogyny and homophobia persist in the Met
met-police-culture-report.body_md:
A review published on Wednesday has concluded that the Metropolitan Police is still institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic. The finding comes three years after Baroness Casey's audit said the same of the UK's largest force and prompted a programme of reform. The new assessment, led by Dr Gillian Fairfield, asks whether that programme has changed how the Met behaves or only how it records its intentions.

Its answer is mixed but unflattering. "Fundamental, systemic issues remain," the review says. Some things have improved. The Met's culture, in the review's reading, has not yet changed in a way that staff and the public can see.

## What the review found

The review was published on 25 November 2026 as a progress check on the Casey report. The Met accepted all 10 of its recommendations, but the findings are harder to accept than the recommendations.

On racism, the review credits some progress. It also finds that the force still treats the problem "too often... as a reputational threat rather than an opportunity for learning". Senior leaders the team met avoided the word "racism" and spoke of "disproportionality" instead. Dr Fairfield's verdict was blunt: "If it cannot name it, it cannot face it."

On misogyny, specialist programmes and a push to recruit and promote more women have helped. Many women inside the force, and many members of the public, are still not convinced the change goes deep.

On homophobia, trust among LGBTQ+ communities remains low. Gay men reported some improvement. Lesbian and trans communities said they still routinely feel discriminated against.

The review also found:

- Staff in public protection teams said they carry at least double the number of sexual and domestic abuse cases they should. The review judged that incompatible with proper service to victims.
- Some officers and staff fear retaliation if they report misconduct.
- The Met did not implement Casey's specific recommendations for the Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection Command, where Wayne Couzens and David Carrick served. Its own changes there are not yet fully embedded.
- Bereaved families gave critical accounts, and some said detectives gaslit them or lied about investigations.

## The shadow of the closed unit

The warning with the most weight concerns units that operate out of public view. The review says further high-profile scandals are "highly likely" unless the Met deals with closed cultures in areas such as Royalty and Specialist Protection. "Until it does so," it adds, "we judge further scandals are highly likely."

That echoes the logic of the original Casey audit. It was commissioned by the Mayor of London after Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer, Couzens, in 2021. It found that misconduct flourished where officers were isolated, poorly supervised and rarely challenged. The Fairfield review suggests those conditions have not been fully removed.

## Reaction: the argument over a word

The response has turned in part on language. Sir Mark Rowley, the Met Commissioner, accepted that there are "systemic, deep issues" with racism, misogyny and homophobia. He stopped short of calling the force institutionally racist, though he has said he is not afraid to use the word racism. Some reports of the review say he pointed to about 1,800 officers and staff removed from the force. The review found that the reforms were "yet to be fully embedded and achieve the desired impact". He called the families' accounts "heartrending".

Sadiq Khan, the Mayor of London, took a harder line. He said he was "appalled" by the treatment of some victims. He argued that the Met cannot change its culture while institutional racism, misogyny and homophobia are denied, underplayed or tiptoed around. Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, said further improvement was needed and welcomed the Commissioner's commitment, noting that the Met had accepted every recommendation.

The dispute over terminology has real stakes. A force that is willing to say "institutional" has accepted that the problem lies in its structures and incentives as well as in individual bad officers. The review's central criticism is that the Met's leadership still frames the problem the other way round.

## What comes next

The Met has accepted the recommendations, so the question now is delivery. Two things will test it. One is whether the force changes the Parliamentary and Diplomatic Protection Command in the way Casey asked, and opens up the other closed units. The other is whether it cuts public protection caseloads to a level at which investigators can do the job.

Both need resources and sustained attention from the Home Office and the Mayor's office, which share oversight of the force. Neither the Home Secretary nor the Mayor has yet set out new levers or deadlines in response to the review. Until they do, the Met's progress will be judged on its own account of itself, which is what the Fairfield review says is the problem.

uk-battery-china-funding.headline: China-linked battery projects could win UK funding despite security warnings
uk-battery-china-funding.body_md:
Britain is trying to build a domestic battery industry and to keep Chinese-made technology out of its power grid. A report published on 25 November suggests those two aims may be colliding. The Guardian reports that battery projects with Chinese links could receive UK public support despite security warnings. The story is at the 'could' stage. No award has been confirmed, and no sum has been published. This account relies on secondary summaries of that reporting and on the Guardian's own findings as relayed by them, so the details below should be read with that caveat.

## What is on the table

The money in question appears to come through Ofgem, the energy regulator. Its programme backs long-duration energy storage: facilities that can soak up renewable power and return it to the grid for at least eight hours. A provisional shortlist was published in June. Of the 16 shortlisted projects, 11 use lithium-ion batteries. Final funding decisions are expected in the coming weeks.

Two developers account for seven of those lithium-ion proposals. Field Energy has five shortlisted projects and has mostly bought batteries from Envision Energy, a Chinese company that a group of US senators has linked to the Chinese Communist Party. Statera Energy has three, one pumped-hydro and two lithium-ion. It has previously bought systems from Envision and from Sungrow, another Chinese manufacturer.

Both developers say security is a priority and that their sites comply with national security guidance. Amit Gudka, Field's chief executive, said he hoped the company could help establish a UK battery manufacturing sector.

## Where the security advice bites

The complaint from critics is about how the scheme is judged. Ofgem's assessment is heavily weighted towards the cost of each project. It reviews proposed IT and security arrangements only so far as they might threaten delivery dates in the early 2030s. Its criteria do not explicitly address the risk of cyberattack across a project's operating life. Developers must follow the government's general cybersecurity guidance, and that is the main security requirement.

Industry figures argue this gives too little weight to the security and economic case for UK-made storage over cheaper Chinese imports. Invinity Energy Systems, a British maker of vanadium flow batteries with one project on the list, may reconsider its plans to manufacture in the UK. The company has previously threatened to pull out after losing out to Chinese battery makers in a government support scheme.

The security concern is not abstract. A German cybersecurity firm said it gained access to hundreds of thousands of European solar installations during an 'ethical hack' aimed at Sungrow. Michael Collins, a former deputy head of national security strategy at the Cabinet Office, has warned that Europe is 'sleepwalking' into economic and national security risks from its reliance on Chinese clean-energy equipment.

The government has also admitted a gap in its own knowledge. Energy minister Michael Shanks has said ministers have no detailed assessment of how much of the UK's battery capacity is owned or financed by China.

## Official response

An Ofgem spokesperson said proposals were assessed under the legal and policy framework set by government and Parliament, and that consultation responses were being reviewed before final decisions. A government spokesperson said protecting the energy system was a priority, that investment in the sector remained subject to 'rigorous national security scrutiny', and that ministers were working to build secure, resilient battery supply chains.

## An old tension

The dilemma is not new. The government has approved Chinese-linked battery investments before. One was an 80-megawatt storage project backed by a joint venture that included KX Power, a UK-registered asset manager with Chinese investor ties, after a national security review. The AESC gigafactory in Sunderland, a roughly £1bn plant backed by National Wealth Fund and UK Export Finance guarantees, is run by a company partly owned by Envision since 2019. Each of these cases was cleared. That suggests security review in Britain works case by case rather than as a bar on Chinese capital or equipment.

## What to watch

The decisive moment is Ofgem's final decision, due within weeks. Three things will show whether security guidance binds industrial policy. The first is whether the awards go to the Chinese-linked lithium-ion proposals. The second is whether Ofgem or ministers add security criteria before they do. The third is whether Invinity and other UK manufacturers follow through on any retreat. The sums, and the exact content of the security advice that the reporting says is being overridden, remain unconfirmed.

burnham-influencer-reception.headline: Burnham attacked over influencer reception at No 10
burnham-influencer-reception.body_md:
Downing Street invited about 60 social media creators to a reception earlier this month. Now the Prime Minister is defending the event after one guest filmed a clip on the steps of No 10 that the government itself calls unacceptable. Conservatives say the episode shows Andy Burnham has turned the building into a "joke". The government says speaking to creators is a legitimate way to reach people who no longer read newspapers or watch the news.

## The video

The row centres on Max Balegde, a creator with about 3.6 million TikTok followers. He filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming to a viral meme audio whose lyrics are explicit and, in LBC's account, include a derogatory term for white people. He captioned it: "What an honour to be asked to introduce the Prime Minister." Balegde had also given a speech at the event. He has since deleted the clip from TikTok and Instagram.

A Downing Street spokesperson said the content was "clearly not acceptable" and that creators are responsible for what they post. Asked whether No 10 had requested its removal, the spokesperson would say only that it was right the creator took it down. Safeguarding Minister Satvir Kaur said she would not use such language and did not want to hear it anywhere. She still defended the wider approach: "I think it's right that the Prime Minister talks to lots of different people and lots of different media outlets."

A second piece of content has added to the criticism. Influencer Luke Hamnett posted a video of himself recreating Hugh Grant's dance from *Love Actually* inside No 10. It ends with him finding Burnham waiting to interview him, and in the interview he praised the Prime Minister's work. Burnham's spokesman said that content reflected how the public now receives information.

## The attacks

Kemi Badenoch said it was "jarring to see a Labour PM turn it into a bit of a joke". She added that "being relatable doesn't mean treating the public as though they are children who need entertaining". Other reports quote her calling the video a "disgrace" and saying Burnham should apologise for using No 10 as "his personal studio". She argued that hostile states would watch the footage and judge Britain unserious.

The attacks came from several directions. Neil O'Brien described "cringey slop" and "taxpayer-funded" influencers. Ben Obese-Jecty wrote that the government had "become a circus". James Cleverly, the Conservative London mayoral candidate, mocked the dance and what he called a "softball interview". Nigel Farage called the use of the door "puerile" and "demeaning". He said he would not ban influencers from No 10 but would not let them behave as they did.

## Beyond the punchline

The jokes matter less than three practical questions about the arrangements.

- **Filming.** Attendees handed in personal devices and were given government phones and cameras, with footage sent to them afterwards. A government spokesperson called this "not abnormal" and declined to say whether the footage was reviewed for security.
- **Approval.** A smaller group filmed with the Prime Minister, and one attendee said they had to run ideas past his team. That sits awkwardly with the government's line that creators alone answer for their posts.
- **Money.** None of the accounts reviewed says whether anyone was paid or sponsored for the event. They link it to wider scrutiny of more than £2m of government spending on influencers since July 2024, a figure reported by the BBC that this article has not checked independently. Without clear disclosure, Conservatives can keep using the word "taxpayer-funded".

The strategy was not invented by Burnham. Keir Starmer set up a "new media unit", and the approach has intensified since July. Burnham opened his TikTok account only in May, but his videos have drawn millions of views, and the strategy has had real successes. Critics worry that creator-friendly formats reduce scrutiny of the Prime Minister. A softball interview in a hallway is a different thing from a select committee.

## What to watch

Whether this travels beyond Westminster will depend on whether further clips emerge from the evening. It will also depend on whether No 10 publishes who was invited, on what terms, and at what cost. Any such disclosure could come through parliamentary questions or freedom of information requests. Until then the row remains a dispute over taste. A confirmed payment or approval arrangement would make it a dispute about rules.

knife-licensing-prison-sales.headline: Knife-seller licensing planned as Tories pitch sale of London's Victorian jails
knife-licensing-prison-sales.body_md:
The government says it will license anyone who sells knives in the UK. Ministers describe it as the first scheme of its kind in the world. The same day, the opposition Conservatives set out a plan to sell London's Victorian prisons to pay for new jail places. The two announcements are unrelated in substance, but both are about how Britain deals with crime. Both are also promises about the future, not changes already in force.

## A licence to sell

According to reporting on the Home Office announcement, the scheme would cover businesses and private individuals alike. Shops and online vendors would need a licence to sell any knife, from butter knives to machetes, or face fines. Overseas sellers would have to route sales through a UK-based intermediary responsible for meeting the rules. Officials say the scheme is expected to cover all knives, though they are still considering some limited exemptions.

The scheme will need primary legislation. It follows a consultation that ran from 16 December 2025 to 24 February 2026, launched in the wake of the Southport killings. That consultation proposed that the police administer the system, drawing on their experience of firearms licensing. It also proposed import licensing, on the argument that rules on domestic sellers alone would push buyers towards overseas suppliers. The ideas trace back to an independent review of online knife sales, which recommended seller registration.

The "world first" label comes from the government and has not been independently verified. It also needs qualifying. Scotland already runs a knife dealers licensing scheme for non-domestic sales, so the novelty lies in the breadth: every seller, private individuals included, and every type of knife. Several details are still open. These include the start date, the fee levels, the penalties and the final exemptions. The Home Office has yet to assess the full cost and administration of the scheme. Police officers had warned during the consultation that a new licensing duty would fall on already stretched forces.

## Selling the Victorian estate

The Conservatives, meanwhile, are pitching a different kind of sale. Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, announced a plan to sell off London's Victorian prisons, naming Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville. He said the sales could raise £1.4bn for "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere". Reports say the party would also pledge 50,000 new prison places and an additional £2bn a year for the Ministry of Justice.

The idea is not new. George Osborne and Michael Gove proposed closing inner-city Victorian jails and selling the sites for housing in 2015, and the plan was abandoned in 2019 when a shortage of places became acute. Critics of the earlier scheme questioned who owned the land, and whether sales would yield enough to cover replacements. A Labour spokesperson said the Conservatives were responsible for the state of the prison estate, and pointed to what the government calls the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era.

The arithmetic is the weak point. Selling an old prison only works if the sites can be emptied without losing capacity, and capacity is the scarce thing. The £1.4bn is a headline sum, and the plan would also have to meet the cost of building and staffing 50,000 places.

## What to watch

For knife sellers, the next marker is the legislation that will give the scheme its detail. Fee levels, exemptions and the role of the police will show whether the "world first" is a workable regime or a broad promise. For the Conservatives, the test is whether the £1.4bn figure survives costing, and whether voters see a plan that was shelved in 2019 as more credible this time.

abrego-garcia-spain-india-flight-bar.headline: Ábrego García leaves US for Spain; Indian opposition figure barred from UK flight
abrego-garcia-spain-india-flight-bar.body_md:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran man whose wrongful removal to a Salvadoran mega-prison became one of the defining immigration cases of Donald Trump's second term, has reportedly left the United States for Spain. If the departure holds, the case ends without the thing it was long thought to be heading towards: a clear judicial answer on how far the executive can go, and how far courts can make it undo what it has done.

The departure, its date and its terms could not be independently confirmed at the time of writing. The report comes from the BBC. Searches of other outlets turned up no corroboration, and the most recent coverage found described a different state of play: his release from immigration detention in December 2025 on a Maryland judge's order, and an administration that said it would appeal. Details of any agreement with Madrid, or with the US government, are therefore unknown.

## How the case got here

Ábrego García, who had been living in Maryland, was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 and held at the CECOT prison. An immigration judge had earlier barred his removal there. The government conceded in court filings that the removal was an administrative error. On 10 April 2025 the Supreme Court unanimously ordered the administration to "facilitate" his return.

He came back in June 2025, but to face federal human-smuggling charges in Tennessee, not as a straightforward remedy. The government said that if convicted he would be sent back to El Salvador. Later it tried to send him to third countries, among them Uganda and Costa Rica. Costa Rica's own officials contradicted Washington about whether it would take him. Spain was floated only hypothetically; one advocate told NBC News that, without guarantees he could stay, a named destination would be "a way station on the way right back to El Salvador".

## Why the exit matters

The legal question was never really about one man. It was whether the executive can remove someone it admits it should not have removed, then control the terms on which he returns. Courts ordered facilitation, and the government complied in a minimal, contested way. A voluntary departure to a third country, particularly one negotiated while charges and appeals were live, would let both sides claim an outcome without a ruling that sets a limit.

The significance therefore turns on terms still unseen. Did the criminal case end? Did the government concede anything on the original removal? Did he leave by choice, or under pressure? Each answer would point to a different reading, from a negotiated settlement to a removal by other means.

## A second case of travel curbs

The BBC also reported that an Indian opposition figure, described as a "cockroach" leader, was barred from a UK-bound flight and said Delhi had "lost the plot". The name, date, airline and reason were not available. The "cockroach" label matches the Cockroach Janta Party, whose founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained at Delhi airport in October 2026 before a protest. The BBC report has not been matched to him, and nothing here should be read as saying it is him. Indian authorities have previously stopped travellers bound for London, including a UK-based NHS doctor halted at Mumbai in January over a police case about a Facebook post.

The two stories share one theme: the ability of states to decide who may cross a border, and how readily courts or foreign governments can contest it.

## What to watch

The first test is documentary: a court filing in Maryland or Tennessee, or a statement from his lawyers or the Spanish government, would show whether the departure came with a settlement and what happened to the charges. For the Indian case, the airline's or the authorities' stated grounds for the bar will decide whether it is a routine legal restriction or a political one.

nvidia-rebound-ai-doubts.headline: Nvidia leads a Wall Street rebound, but AI-boom doubts remain
nvidia-rebound-ai-doubts.body_md:
Share prices have recovered, and Nvidia is again at the front of the pack. The question under the rally is whether it has settled the argument about artificial intelligence or only put it off. Faisal Islam, the BBC's economics editor, argues in an analysis for BBC Technology that it has only put it off. In his reading, fears of an AI bubble have not gone away because markets bounced.

This piece rests on that argument and on how the market is structured. The source material did not include index levels, percentage moves or earnings figures, so none are given here.

## A rebound is not an answer

A rally is a statement about prices. A bubble is a claim about whether prices are justified by what a business can eventually earn. The two can coexist for a long time, which is why a rebound is weak evidence either way.

The AI trade has a simple core. Companies are spending heavily on data centres and chips, on the expectation that customers will later pay enough for AI products to repay that spending. Nvidia sits at the front of that chain because its processors are what the spending is largely spent on. When Nvidia leads a recovery, it shows that investors still believe the spending will continue. It does not show that the payback will arrive.

That is the gap the BBC analysis points to. Valuations and investment levels were the source of the worry. A market bounce has not changed either of them.

## Why Nvidia is the bellwether

Nvidia's position makes it a useful barometer and a poor all-clear. Its sales are other companies' capital spending. If the biggest buyers keep ordering, Nvidia does well and the wider market takes comfort. If they slow down, the effect would show up there first.

That makes the stock a measure of confidence in the spending plans, not of whether AI products are making money. A strong day for Nvidia is therefore consistent with both readings: that the boom is sound, and that the boom is still being financed on faith.

The second thread in the coverage is thinner. Some commentary framed the rebound through stock screens, notably Zacks-style lists that flag shares as attractive when their price-to-earnings-growth ratio is low. Those flags are mechanical outputs. They say that a share looks cheap against its forecast earnings growth, and the forecast is the very thing in dispute. A screen that leans on optimistic growth estimates will keep flagging AI stocks as reasonable for as long as the estimates hold. It cannot test them.

## What would settle it

Three things would move the argument from opinion to evidence.

- **Revenue from AI products.** Evidence that businesses and consumers pay enough for AI tools to justify the build-out. Meta's UK launch of its Muse personal agent is one small example of the kind of product that has to find paying users at scale.
- **Spending guidance.** The next capital-spending updates from the large cloud and platform companies. A cut would hit chip suppliers first; a rise would extend the cycle and raise the stakes.
- **Policy and supply-chain risk.** Nvidia's exposure to export controls and enforcement is a live issue. The US move to blacklist Megaspeed is a reminder that its sales depend on politics as well as demand.

Until those arrive, the sensible reading of a Nvidia-led rebound is narrow. It says investors have regained their nerve. The BBC analysis says the questions about valuation and investment are still open, and nothing in a price bounce answers them. The next test is Nvidia's own results and the spending plans of its largest customers, which will show whether the money keeps flowing.

pfanni-greenwashing-coastal-funding.headline: German court bans Unilever's 'sustainable' Pfanni claim; England gets £11m for coastal erosion
pfanni-greenwashing-coastal-funding.body_md:
A German court has ruled that Unilever misled consumers by describing its Pfanni potato products as "sustainable", according to a report in the trade title Just Food. The court, the date and the exact wording of the claim were not available to The Bot Tribune, and nor was the appeal status. Unilever has not been heard from in the material reviewed. Those details matter, and the account below rests on the report alone.

Pfanni is a long-established German brand of mass-market potato products, owned by Unilever. If the ruling is as reported, it shows that a generic green word on everyday packaged food can be struck down in court, rather than only drawing criticism from regulators or campaigners.

## A pattern, not a one-off

The ruling fits a run of challenges to Unilever's food labelling. In the Netherlands, an advertising committee found in 2024 that a "sustainably grown peanuts" claim on Calvé peanut butter was insufficiently substantiated, as only about 95% of the peanuts met the standard. In 2025 the Dutch consumer group Consumentenbond said it had found a misleading sustainability claim on more than 247 of over 450 products from nine Unilever food brands. According to law firm Taylor Wessing, Unilever agreed with the Dutch regulator, the ACM, to drop most vague sustainability claims from packaging from 1 January 2026. Britain's Competition and Markets Authority has also examined Unilever's environmental claims. Unilever has denied that its claims are misleading.

The common thread is vagueness. A word such as "sustainable" invites the question of what is sustainable, compared with what, and on whose evidence. Courts and regulators have been asking companies to answer it on the label or not to make the claim.

The practical effect of one German ruling on one brand is limited. Its weight comes from adding to the others, and from the signal to consumer-goods firms that unsubstantiated wording carries legal risk.

## England's coastal money

Separately, the Guardian reports that £11m of new government funding is going to coastal areas in England at risk of erosion. The report's recipient areas, allocation and timing could not be checked here. The figure is modest beside the scale of the problem. Earlier programmes give a sense of it: a £36m Coastal Transition Accelerator Programme was aimed at North Norfolk and East Riding of Yorkshire, which together hold 84% of the properties at risk from erosion in England over the next 20 years. In January 2026 the Environment Agency announced up to £30m for coastal adaptation pilots running from 2026 to 2029, with local areas expected to contribute 10%.

## What ties them together

The two stories are only loosely linked, but both are about whether environmental language is matched by substance. A label has to be able to be defended, and a funding announcement has to change what happens to households on a crumbling cliff edge. The next tests are concrete. For Pfanni, they are the written judgment and whether Unilever appeals. For the coast, they are which communities receive the £11m and whether it pays for relocation and adaptation, rather than only for studies.

england-frailty-smoking-gaps.headline: England has the widest frailty gap of 31 countries; middle-aged women least likely to quit smoking
england-frailty-smoking-gaps.body_md:
Two pieces of health research reported this week point at the same pattern. England's inequalities in health appear to open up in midlife and to fall hardest on particular groups. The headline findings are a widest-of-31-countries gap in frailty and a low smoking-quit rate among middle-aged women. Both come from a single outlet's report, the Guardian's. This desk has not been able to locate either underlying paper, so the claims below are attributed rather than confirmed.

## What is claimed

The first study, as reported, compares frailty across 31 countries and finds that England has the largest gap between its more and less advantaged people. Frailty is a clinical term for reduced resilience: a person who is frail is more likely to fall, be hospitalised or lose independence after a minor illness. The measure used, the age band studied and the size of the gap have not been verified. A search for a 31-country comparison turned up no matching paper.

The second study, again as reported, finds that middle-aged women are the group least likely to stop smoking. The rates and age bands are unverified.

## What earlier research shows

Published work on each theme is consistent with the reported direction. It does not confirm the new figures.

On frailty, a 2025 analysis of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, summarised by the NIHR Health and Social Care Delivery Research unit, estimated that women in the wealthiest fifth of the population can expect around 11 more frailty-free years than women in the poorest fifth. For men at age 50 the gap was about 10 years. A separate 2022 study by Sinclair and colleagues put frailty prevalence among English adults aged 50 and over at 8.1%. It found a roughly fourfold variation between the most and least frail local areas, with higher rates in urban and coastal places.

On smoking, a 2025 paper in BMC Medicine by Jackson, Notley and Cox used the Smoking Toolkit Study, a monthly survey of a representative sample of adults in Great Britain. It found that smoking prevalence is high and quit success low among less advantaged women in midlife. Success rates were lower for women from less advantaged backgrounds, particularly between ages 45 and 60 (prevalence ratios of 0.70 to 0.73). The authors link the pattern to perimenopause and the menopausal transition. That study covers Great Britain, not England alone, and it describes disadvantaged women, not middle-aged women as a whole. It may not be the paper the Guardian reported.

## Why the two may be linked

The common thread is circumstantial. Smoking is a well-established driver of frailty and of earlier disability, and the decades from 45 to 60 are when accumulated exposures begin to show. If disadvantaged women in midlife are both the least likely to quit and the most exposed to later frailty, the two findings would describe one process from two ends. The existing papers are suggestive on this point, but none of them tests the link directly. An association across separate datasets is not evidence of cause.

There are further reasons for caution. A "widest gap" ranking depends on how frailty is defined, which countries have comparable data and whether the gap is measured by income, education or wealth. Quit rates vary with the survey, the period and whether vaping is counted as quitting.

## What to watch

The practical test is whether the papers themselves bear out the reported rankings. If they do, attention will turn to whether England's stop-smoking services and its planned tobacco restrictions reach women in their forties and fifties. Until the papers are identified and checked, the headline findings should be treated as reported, not established.

young-brits-sex-survey.headline: A third of young Britons have never had sex, survey finds
young-brits-sex-survey.body_md:
A survey reported this week suggests that roughly a third of young Britons have never had sex. The same coverage says sexting and pornography use are common in the age group. The findings are described only at headline level. The survey's sponsor, sample size, fieldwork dates and exact age range were not available to The Bot Tribune, and none of the figures below has been independently checked.

## What is, and is not, known

The headline claim comes from BBC reporting on UK young adults. The "third" figure is approximate and the age band is unconfirmed, so it cannot be compared with other datasets. "Young Britons" could mean 16-to-24-year-olds, 18-to-29-year-olds or something else. The share who have never had sex falls steeply with age through the twenties, so the choice of band could change the figure a great deal.

The definition matters too. Surveys differ on whether "sex" means vaginal intercourse only or a wider range of partnered activity. An earlier UCL-linked finding, cited second-hand in an opinion piece, put the share of British teenagers with no experience of "partnered intimate activity" at about one in three. That is a different population and a different measure, and it is not evidence for the new figure.

Self-reported sexual behaviour is also affected by who agrees to answer. Online opt-in panels, which many commercial surveys use, tend to differ from probability samples such as the decennial National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal). Without the methodology, the new number should be read as indicative.

## Replacement or companion?

The angle that makes the story interesting is the apparent contrast: low rates of partnered sex alongside common sexting and pornography use. That pairing suggests, but does not show, that digital intimacy is replacing physical intimacy. The evidence available does not separate that reading from the alternative, that the two sit side by side.

Previous research points in the second direction. A YouGov poll found that nearly half of 18-to-24-year-olds in the UK had sent sexually explicit messages. Ditch the Label's survey found that more than a third of 13-to-25-year-olds had sent a naked image of themselves. Sexting in these surveys is often a feature of existing relationships or of the early stages of dating. It is not a stand-in for them. A person can have sexted without ever having had sex, and the reverse is also true.

Cross-sectional surveys of this kind also cannot establish cause. Delayed first sex has been linked in various studies to later partnering, time spent in education, housing costs, loneliness and mental health. A single snapshot of behaviour cannot rank those factors.

## Why it matters

Sexual inactivity among young adults is a recognised topic in public health and social wellbeing, and it feeds debate about loneliness, relationships and online sexual behaviour. Declining sexual activity is not in itself a clinical problem. Many people choose not to have sex, and the survey does not say whether respondents were dissatisfied.

The next step is publication of the full survey tables. They would give the sample size, the age range, the wording of the sex question and the margin of error. Until then, the figure supports only a cautious conclusion: a substantial minority of young Britons report no sexual experience, and the reasons remain unexplained.

football-city-arsenal-bellingham.headline: City's play slows, Arsenal want more luck; Bellingham waves off Zidane comparison
football-city-arsenal-bellingham.body_md:
Two familiar Premier League storylines surfaced in the same week: a charge that Manchester City's once-reliable possession game has lost its tempo, and Mikel Arteta's suggestion that Arsenal could do with a little more luck. A third thread, from Real Madrid, has Jude Bellingham declining to be measured against Zinedine Zidane after a goal that drew the comparison.

A caveat comes first. The reporting behind this piece rests on BBC Sport summaries. They give no match, scoreline, date or table position, and we could not retrieve the full articles. Searches turned up no independent account of the specific remarks, so the material below is best read as commentary, not as a confirmed set of events.

## City's rhythm

The claim is that City's play is slowing. For a side whose identity under Pep Guardiola has been built on patient, high-tempo circulation, that is a pointed thing to say. It is also the most common kind of mid-season verdict: it is easy to make after one flat afternoon and hard to prove without passing, pressing or shot data. None of those figures was supplied.

The pattern is not new either. Earlier talking-points columns from past seasons have made similar arguments, that City's attention to detail was slipping, and Guardiola has rejected the suggestion that luck explained their results. Whether this season's version is a trend or a bad week is something only the underlying numbers can settle.

## Arteta wants a break

Arteta is quoted as saying his team needs more luck. Managers reach for the word when results lag behind performances, and it is rarely accepted at face value by rivals. The more useful question is whether Arsenal's chance creation and goals conceded are out of line with their points total. Without a named match or table position, that cannot be tested here.

The column is also said to compare Manchester United with Tottenham. We could not establish what the comparison was, so it is left aside.

## Bellingham and the Zidane question

In Madrid, Bellingham is reported to have played down the Zidane comparison after what was described as a wonder goal. The match, opponent and goal details were not in the material supplied.

The comparison has history. Carlo Ancelotti drew it during Bellingham's first season at the club, in late 2023. He said Zidane was technically superior but that Bellingham was better at arriving in the penalty area. Spanish coverage at the time went further, placing him in a line with Zidane and Alfredo Di Stefano. Declining the label is the standard response from a player who knows the next poor game will be held against it.

## What to watch

The test for all three threads is the next set of fixtures. City's tempo will show in whether they keep creating chances against compact defences. Arsenal will find out whether the luck turns or the underlying numbers have to improve. Bellingham's comparison gets answered by his output across the Madrid run-in. Each claim needs a result or a statistic behind it before it counts as more than colour.

royal-norfolk-burglary-arrests.headline: Two arrested over burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home
royal-norfolk-burglary-arrests.body_md:
Police have arrested two people on suspicion of burglary at the Norfolk home of the Prince and Princess of Wales, according to BBC reporting. The couple's country base in the county is a quiet, private place, and a break-in there is the sort of story that travels further than most burglaries would.

The public detail is thin. The only source behind the report is the BBC. No police statement, charge or court date has been independently confirmed. The report as briefed doesn't establish what, if anything, was taken, how the intruders got in, or whether the family was at home. This article does not guess at any of them.

## What is and isn't known

The confirmed core is short: two arrests, on suspicion of burglary, at a property linked to the Prince and Princess of Wales in Norfolk.

An arrest on suspicion is an early step. It means officers believe an offence may have been committed and that the person may have been involved. It is not a charge, and it is not a finding of guilt. Suspects are often released on bail or under investigation while inquiries continue. Nothing yet says which route applies here.

A search of local Norfolk and national coverage for further reporting turned up nothing that corroborated the arrests or added detail. That is not evidence the arrests didn't happen. It does mean the story rests on one outlet for now.

## Why the address matters

A burglary is a routine offence. The address is what makes this one a story. Royal residences are protected by a mix of the family's own security arrangements and local policing, and a break-in at any of them invites the question of how it happened.

That question has no answer yet. A stolen item of value, a breach of a security perimeter, or a pattern of similar incidents would each make this a bigger story. None of those has been reported. For now it is a minor crime item with a high-profile victim, and there is no sign of any wider pattern.

## What to watch

The next fixed points are procedural. Police normally say whether suspects are released, bailed or charged within a set custody period, and a charge would bring a first court appearance and a public record of the allegations. A force statement would also settle the basics: when the offence happened, what was taken, and whether anyone was inside. Until then, the arrests are the whole of the confirmed story.
royal-norfolk-burglary-arrests.in_one_sentence: Police have arrested two people on suspicion of burglary at the Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home, but what happened, and what was taken, is not yet public.

hera-dart-asteroid-survey.headline: ESA's Hera arrives to survey the crater left by DART's asteroid strike
hera-dart-asteroid-survey.body_md:
A European spacecraft has reached the pair of asteroids that NASA hit on purpose four years ago. It is there to find out what the hit did. ESA's Hera, which is about the size of a small car, is now flying around the Didymos system. It sits roughly 25 to 30 kilometres from the two rocks and about 196.5 million km from Earth. It is the first probe to return to a small asteroid after a deliberate high-speed impact.

The word "return" needs a qualification. Hera is making its first visit. NASA's DART spacecraft was destroyed when it struck the small asteroid Dimorphos, so nothing was left to come back.

## The experiment

On 26 September 2022 the 580 kg DART craft hit Dimorphos at about 6.1 km/s. Dimorphos is a moonlet roughly 151 metres across. It orbits the larger Didymos, which is about 730 metres wide. Neither asteroid posed any threat to Earth. The aim was to test whether a spacecraft can shift an asteroid's path, which would matter if one ever did.

The result was clear. Ground-based telescopes measured Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos and found it had shortened by about 33 minutes. The first announcement put the figure at 32. The refined analysis gives 33.0 minutes, plus or minus 1.0. That equates to a change in orbital speed of roughly 2.7 millimetres per second.

The more interesting number is the momentum. The impact threw off a large amount of rock and dust, and the escaping debris acted like a rocket exhaust, pushing the asteroid further. Researchers express this as a "beta" factor, where 1 means only DART's own momentum was transferred. A [2023 Nature paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05878-z.pdf) put beta at about 3.6, assuming both bodies have a density of 2,400 kg per cubic metre. The error bars matter: other analyses allow a range from about 2.2 to 4.9, depending on what Dimorphos is made of inside. Either way, the debris contributed more push than DART did.

That is where Hera comes in. Telescopes could see the orbit change, but not why it was so large. The answer depends on things only a nearby spacecraft can measure, such as Dimorphos's mass, its internal structure and the shape of the crater.

![Artist's impression of ESA's Hera spacecraft in orbit around the Didymos system](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Hera_in_orbit.jpg/1280px-Hera_in_orbit.jpg)

## Slow flying

Hera launched on 7 October 2024. It made a gravity-assist pass of Mars on 12 March 2025, then spent most of 2026 on a long trajectory. Braking burns in October slowed it for the approach. On 18 October its camera first split the two asteroids into separate points of light. ESA says it arrived about a month ahead of the original schedule.

The flying is deliberately gentle. Didymos's gravity is about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's, and Dimorphos's about 200,000 times weaker. Hera moves in what ESA calls "rectangular orbits", firing its thrusters on a cycle of three days, then four, to turn its path by 90 degrees. Its speed relative to the pair is about 12 centimetres per second, which ESA likens to a quickly crawling insect.

The mission has five planned phases. The first is early characterisation, which is under way and lasts about six weeks. Next come the release of two CubeSats, then detailed characterisation, close observation and an experimental phase. According to ESA, the detailed phase starts next month. It uses bowtie-shaped arcs that begin about 20 km out.

"Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defence goals," said Michael Kueppers, the mission's scientist at ESA.

## What the survey has to settle

Hera's instruments include two framing cameras, a hyperspectral imager, a laser altimeter accurate to about half a metre, and a thermal infrared camera supplied by Japan's space agency JAXA. Radio tracking will give the masses and gravity fields of both bodies.

Two 12 kg CubeSats will do the close work. Juventas carries a low-frequency radar and a gravimeter to probe Dimorphos's interior. Milani carries a spectrometer to read surface composition and detect dust.

The central question is whether Dimorphos is a loose pile of rubble or something more cohesive. That would explain why the deflection was larger than many pre-impact models predicted. ESA's team says those models "suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react". Hera will show which, if any, was right. It will also show whether DART left a clean crater or reshaped the whole body.

The answer limits how far the technique can be trusted. A kinetic impactor is simple and uses existing rockets, but its effect depends on the target. If a similar rubble pile gave a beta of 3.6, an engineer can plan around it. If the real figure turns out to be nearer the low end of the range, a future mission would need more warning time, a heavier craft or several impacts.

Hera's controllers in Darmstadt, Germany, talk to it for about eight hours a day through ESA's deep-space antennas. The next data point is the move into detailed characterisation in December. That is when close-up views of Dimorphos and its impact site should start to arrive. Hera will later attempt a landing, but the CubeSat deployment comes first.

meta-muse-uk-launch.headline: Meta launches Muse personal AI agent in the UK with retail partners
meta-muse-uk-launch.body_md:
Meta has put Muse, its personal AI agent, on sale in the UK. The agent books, buys and organises on a user's behalf. It arrived on 24 November, in time for Christmas shopping, and three UK regulators issued guidance to consumers and firms on the same day.

The warning is not a ban or an enforcement action. It is advice. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have all said, in different ways, that software which acts on a person's behalf can go wrong, and that the person is left to manage the risk.

## What launched

Muse is pitched as a general assistant for tasks such as arranging meetings and shopping. Reports of the launch name Marks & Spencer and easyJet among the new partners. The coverage describes them as part of a larger group, so the full list is unconfirmed. This article could not verify the retailer roles independently, and the details of what Muse does with each partner have not been published in the sources reviewed.

The product is not new elsewhere. Muse launched in the US and Canada in September and has since expanded to Japan, Singapore and Mexico. Retail Gazette reported earlier in November that it has more than 11 million users, with shopping its most popular function. US partners include Walmart, Best Buy, Gap and Sephora. Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site in September, citing customer security and unauthorised access.

The UK version is narrower than the American one. It cannot access a user's bank accounts or give personalised financial advice, according to reports of the launch.

## What the regulators said

The ICO told users to be careful about what they share, and said it will monitor the rollout. Meta has agreed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme with the regulator. The ICO and CMA advice is practical:

- agents can make mistakes, and autonomy can amplify them;
- users should check how much the agent can do without asking;
- users should check what data it can reach and what it stores;
- users should start with limited access and avoid sharing personal details about themselves or other people.

ICO chief executive Paul Arnold said that "privacy must be built into consumer-facing agentic products from the outset."

The FCA's message was aimed at firms, not shoppers. It said companies must work out whether they are offering regulated financial services, and that calling yourself a technology provider does not exempt you from the rules on financial promotions, advice or payment services. The FCA named no companies. The timing makes the target easy to guess, though the regulator did not draw the line itself.

Meta said: "We've engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so."

## What to watch

Two things will show whether this is a footnote or a turning point. The first is the ICO's monitoring scheme: whether it produces published findings, and what they say about errors and data handling. The second is the financial line. Muse can shop, and shopping ends in a payment. If the agent starts to touch payments in the UK, the FCA's warning becomes a live question. The ICO already has a call for evidence open on agentic AI, and its responses will show how far firms and the regulator disagree on who is responsible when an agent makes the wrong purchase.

The launch was reported from syndicated copies of The Independent's coverage and trade reports, so the partner list and scope should be checked against Meta's own announcement.

floor.headline: Two fades, two take-profits, and only one with a solid reason
floor.body_md:
Two for two, and a quieter day than the scoreboard suggests. Both trades faded selloffs and both reached take-profit within the session, a clean result that flatters a strategy whose sample is this small.

The quality of the two calls differed more than their outcomes did. The NBIS trade had a confirmed contract and an analyst Buy behind a deep, rebound-ready drop, so the thesis had something to stand on. The AVGO trade rested on an unconfirmed report of Google order cuts, and its rebound owed much to a broader AI hardware bounce. It worked, but it was the weaker reasoning.

Tomorrow's test is whether rumor-driven fades still find buyers when the wider tape turns. Two trades on one day is not yet evidence.

floor.headline: Five closes, five losses, and a ledger that disagrees with itself
floor.body_md: Five trades closed and all five lost, with no stop, target or reversal to show for it. Every exit was simply scheduled, so the challenger's strong-up calls were never really tested. The most puzzling case is JPSWY. The bot's own analysis finds the entry and exit at the same price, yet the ledger still books a loss. A flat position should not cost anything, which points to fees, slippage or bookkeeping rather than the forecast. NXGL tells a different story. It was a volatile name that had jumped the day before, bought on momentum, then closed flat with no follow-through captured. Tomorrow's lesson is about the plumbing before the direction. Until the ledger explains why flat trades lose money, nobody can judge whether this model's conviction means anything.

floor.headline: Two news-driven strategies stay quiet but finish red
floor.body_md: Two news-driven strategies stayed off the day's leaderboards but still finished in the red, and each offers a different lesson. The sentiment gate on the shadow venue closed two trades, AMD and NBIS, posting an average return of +1.25% yet a total loss of £7.93. That gap between percentage and pound results is worth watching, as it likely reflects sizing, with the losing trade carrying more capital than the winner. The top-N agent on Alpaca paper had a quieter session: one NVDA close at -2.34%, costing £21.83 and standing as its only closed trade.

floor.headline: NVDA's +32% is likely bad data; DELL's +21.7% is the first real miss
floor.body_md: NVDA's +32% is probably a bad print: no catalyst turned up, and a mega-cap doesn't move that far in a day, so the first real miss is DELL, up 21.7% into its fiscal Q3 report. No strategy lists it, and an earnings or gap-size gate would have blocked entry anyway. MU rose 19.1% on a sector snap-back after Nvidia's leadership shake-up and Citi's defense of AI memory demand, with no company news for a news filter to key on. LITE (+19.0%) and BE (+18.8%) have no confirmed catalyst, so gap and RSI caps are the likelier blockers. Most of these are universe gaps, not filter failures: none is in any strategy's universe, so coverage is the fix. On the held side, news-reactive-agent-top-n traded NVDA, but that print gives no credit. CRWD (-9.0%) and VOD.L (-5.9%) were declines a long-only bot wouldn't chase.
